claims.source: After measuring a dose-response curve by varying the concentration of DAMGO, we found that the IC50 values at +80 mV and −80 mV did not differ, providing an indication that inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation was voltage-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that IC50 values did not differ at different voltages.

claims.claim: Currents evoked by TRPM3 agonists in isolated DRG neurons were rapidly (less than 5 s) inhibited by µOR activation.
claims.source: Similarly, performing patch-clamp experiments on isolated DRG neurons, we observed that the currents evoked by TRPM3 agonists were rapidly (less than 5 s) inhibited by µOR activation (Figure 2a–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2a-c, which shows electrophysiological recordings from DRG neurons.

claims.claim: Upon washout of DAMGO, the inhibition of TRPM3 currents was at least partially reversible.
claims.source: Upon washout of DAMGO, the inhibition was at least partially reversible.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claims.claim: Application of the µOR agonist DAMGO did not evoke outward currents in isolated DRG neurons.
claims.source: Aiming for small-diameter nociceptors, we selected cells that responded either to TRPV1- or to TRPM3-activating (or to both types of) agonists. In these cells, we could not detect outward currents upon application of the µOR agonist DAMGO (Figure 2d–f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2d-f, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The reduction of PS-induced currents by µOR activation is not due to the activation of outward currents.
claims.source: This indicates that the reduction of PS-induced currents by µOR activation is not due to the activation of outward currents.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DAMGO did not evoke outward currents.

claims.claim: The DAMGO-induced reduction of PS-evoked Ca2+ signals is unlikely to be caused by K+ channel-dependent hyperpolarization.
claims.source: Consequently, the DAMGO-induced reduction of PS-evoked Ca2+ signals observed in Ca2+ imaging experiments (e.g. in Figure 1a–g) is unlikely to be caused by K+ channel-dependent hyperpolarization.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DAMGO did not activate K+ channels (outward currents).

claims.claim: TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons are inhibited by activating µORs.
claims.source: Together, these data argue that TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons are inhibited by activating µORs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: 91.5% (562 of 614) of the PS-sensitive neurons were inhibited by DAMGO.
claims.source: Overall, 91.5% (562 of 614) of the PS-sensitive neurons were inhibited by DAMGO.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claims.claim: Most neurons (465 of 562 cells, 83%), which showed a reduction of TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals due to application of DAMGO, also showed capsaicin-induced Ca2+ signals, demonstrating the presence of functional TRPV1 channels.
claims.source: In agreement with this, we found that most neurons (465 of 562 cells, 83%), which showed a reduction of TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals due to application of DAMGO, also showed capsaicin-induced Ca2+ signals, demonstrating the presence of functional TRPV1 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claims.claim: Only a minority of the cells without apparent effect of DAMGO on TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals (14 of 52 DAMGO-insensitive cells, i.e. 27% of the DAMGO-insensitive cells, corresponding to 2% of all PS-sensitive cells) showed a response to capsaicin.
claims.source: Conversely, only a minority of the cells without apparent effect of DAMGO on TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals (14 of 52 DAMGO-insensitive cells, i.e. 27% of the DAMGO-insensitive cells, corresponding to 2% of all PS-sensitive cells) showed a response to capsaicin (Figure 2i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claims.claim: Activation of µORs is capable of rapidly and strongly reducing currents through TRPM3 channels in a subset of DRG neurons, corresponding largely, but not exclusively, to putative peptidergic nociceptors.
claims.source: Together, these data show that activation of µORs is capable of rapidly and strongly reducing currents through TRPM3 channels in a subset of DRG neurons, corresponding largely, but not exclusively, to putative peptidergic nociceptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the correlation between DAMGO sensitivity and capsaicin sensitivity.

claims.claim: All GPCRs that couple to Gi/o proteins inhibited TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons.
claims.source: We therefore tested other GPCRs that couple to Gαi-containing G proteins and found that all of them inhibited TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons, although the number of neurons responding to the specific agonists was variable (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements with various GPCR agonists.

claims.claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating CB2 cannabinoid receptors.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating δ-opioid receptors.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating adrenoreceptors.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating somatostatin receptors.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: When metabotropic glutamate type five receptors (mGluR5) were activated, the weakest inhibition of all agonists was observed, which was only detectable in a relatively small number of neurons.
claims.source: When we activated metabotropic glutamate type five receptors (mGluR5), which preferentially couple to Gαq proteins (Bhave et al., 2001) we observed the weakest inhibition of all agonists, which was only detectable in a relatively small number of neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3f, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The weak inhibition caused by DHPG did not recover upon washout.
claims.source: In addition, the weak inhibition caused by DHPG did not recover upon washout (Figure 3f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3f, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The activity of TRPM3 channels can be inhibited by a large variety of Gαi-coupled GPCRs.
claims.source: These data show that the activity of TRPM3 channels can be inhibited by a large variety of Gαi-coupled GPCRs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that multiple Gαi-coupled GPCRs inhibit TRPM3 channels.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signals induced by the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin showed the same reduction in activity whether DAMGO or the solvent control (DMSO) was applied to the DRG neurons.
claims.source: Ca2+ signals induced by the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin showed the same reduction in activity whether DAMGO or the solvent control (DMSO) was applied to the DRG neurons (Figure 4a,b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: When DAMGO was co-applied together with longer applied capsaicin, there was a much weaker inhibition compared to the inhibition typically observed with TRPM3.
claims.source: Furthermore, when we used a different protocol and co-applied DAMGO together with longer applied capsaicin, there was a much weaker inhibition compared to the inhibition typically observed with TRPM3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were not subject to inhibition by DAMGO, regardless of whether the neurons were PS-sensitive or not.
claims.source: Similarly to our results with TRPV1, we observed that AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were not subject to inhibition by DAMGO, regardless of whether the neurons were PS-sensitive or not (Figure 4c,d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4c,d, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: In HEK cells overexpressing TRPV1 channels together with µORs, there was no evidence for any inhibitory action of µORs on TRPV1 channels in the time frame investigated (2 min).
claims.source: When we overexpressed TRPV1 channels together with µORs in HEK cells, we found no evidence for any inhibitory action of µORs on TRPV1 channels in the time frame investigated (2 min; Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4e, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: In overexpression systems, there was no indication of inhibitory action of µORs on TRPA1 channels.
claims.source: Similarly, we investigated the coupling of µORs to TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels in overexpression systems, again without finding any indication of inhibitory action of µORs on these channels (Figure 4f,g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4f, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: In overexpression systems, there was no indication of inhibitory action of µORs on TRPM8 channels.
claims.source: Similarly, we investigated the coupling of µORs to TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels in overexpression systems, again without finding any indication of inhibitory action of µORs on these channels (Figure 4f,g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4g, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: From the group of TRP channels implicated in noxious thermoreception and inflammatory hyperalgesia, only TRPM3 channels displayed a substantial, rapid and reversible inhibition during µOR activation.
claims.source: In summary, from the group of TRP channels implicated in noxious thermoreception and inflammatory hyperalgesia, only TRPM3 channels displayed a substantial, rapid and reversible inhibition during µOR activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRPV1, TRPA1, and TRPM8 channels were not substantially inhibited by µOR activation, while TRPM3 channels were.

claims.claim: PTX treatment strongly reduced the action of DAMGO on PS-evoked activity in DRG neurons.
claims.source: We tested whether Gi/o proteins were involved in the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels by incubating cultured DRG neurons for 16–24 hr with pertussis toxin (PTX), which selectively disrupts signaling via Gi/o proteins (Mangmool and Kurose, 2011). We found that this treatment strongly reduced the action of DAMGO on PS-evoked activity in DRG neurons (Figure 5a,b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: In HEK cells overexpressing µORs and TRPM3 proteins, PTX treatment almost completely abrogated the DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: Moreover, in HEK cells overexpressing µORs and TRPM3 proteins, PTX treatment almost completely abrogated the DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 channels (Figure 5c,d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5c,d, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The classical signaling pathway comprising G proteins containing Gαi/o subunits is strongly implicated in the inhibition of TRPM3.
claims.source: These data strongly implicate the classical signaling pathway comprising G proteins containing Gαi/o subunits in the inhibition of TRPM3.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that PTX, which disrupts Gi/o signaling, reduces the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claims.claim: Application of forskolin together with IBMX did not prevent the action of DAMGO in isolated DRG neurons.
claims.source: We found that application of IBMX (to inhibit cAMP-degrading phosphodiesterases) and forskolin (to stimulate cAMP-producing adenylyl cyclases) did not influence TRPM3 channel activity in DRG neurons nor their inhibition by µOR activation (Figure 5e,f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5e,f, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Combined application of forskolin and IBMX did not influence TRPM3 channel activity in TRPM3- and µOR-overexpressing HEK cells nor their inhibition by µOR activation.
claims.source: We observed the same outcome in TRPM3- and µOR-overexpressing HEK cells after combined application of forskolin and IBMX (Figure 5g,h).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5g,h, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: When TRPM3- and µOR-expressing HEK cells were dialyzed with the unhydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP through the pipette in patch-clamp experiments, there was no evidence that this treatment affected the inhibitory action of µOR activation on TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: However, when we dialyzed TRPM3- and µOR-expressing HEK cells with the unhydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP through the pipette in patch-clamp experiments, effectively blocking the action of all kinases, including PKAs, we found no evidence that this treatment affected the inhibitory action of µOR activation on TRPM3 channels (Figure 5i,k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5i,k, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: When Mg2+ ions were removed from the intracellular solution, the inhibiting action of DAMGO on TRPM3 channel activity was lost after 5 min of internally dialyzing the cells via the patch pipette.
claims.source: On the other hand, when we removed Mg2+ ions from the intracellular solution, the inhibiting action of DAMGO on TRPM3 channel activity was lost after 5 min of internally dialyzing the cells via the patch pipette (Figure 5j,k and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5j,k and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: µOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition relies on G-protein signaling as G proteins need Mg2+ ions to bind GTP.
claims.source: These data also support our earlier conclusion that µOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition relies on G-protein signaling as G proteins need Mg2+ ions to bind GTP (Gilman, 1987).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removing Mg2+ ions abolishes the inhibition, combined with the knowledge that G proteins need Mg2+ to bind GTP.

claims.claim: Kinases are not involved in the signaling pathway of µORs to TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: Therefore, these experiments suggest that kinases are not involved in the signaling pathway of µORs to TRPM3 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking kinases with AMP-PNP did not affect the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claims.claim: None of the pharmacological kinase inhibitors (H89, KT5720, BIM) abolished the inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation.
claims.source: This conclusion was further corroborated by experiments using kinase inhibitors (H89, a relatively non-specific kinase inhibitor (Lochner and Moolman, 2006); KT5720, inhibitor of PKA; BIM, inhibitor of PKC), none of which abolished the inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6, which shows experimental measurements with kinase inhibitors.

claims.claim: TRPM3 inhibition after µOR activation is a G-protein-coupled process, but does not involve the second messenger cAMP or downstream kinases.
claims.source: Taken together, these data (Figures 5 and 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) strongly indicate that TRPM3 inhibition after µOR activation is a G-protein-coupled process, but does not involve the second messenger cAMP or downstream kinases.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that manipulating cAMP levels and blocking kinases did not affect the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claims.claim: Overexpression of each of the three Gαi proteins, either in wild-type form or as constitutively active QtoL mutant of Gαi1, had no inhibitory effect on the activity of TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: We overexpressed Gα or Gβγ subunits together with TRPM3 channels in HEK cells and assessed their activity by applying PS. Overexpression of each of the three Gαi proteins, either in wild-type form (Figure 7a), or as constitutively active QtoL mutant (Graziano and Gilman, 1989) of Gαi1 (Figure 7b) had no inhibitory effect on the activity of TRPM3 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: YFP-tagged Gαi subunits failed to inhibit TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: We also tested YFP-tagged Gαi subunits (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a), because these allowed to easily assess the expression of the proteins by fluorescence microscopy. These tagged Gαi subunits also failed to inhibit TRPM3 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Gαo1 did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
claims.source: Equally to the Gαi subunits, overexpression of Gαo1 (Figure 7c) or Gαo2 (Figure 7d) did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7c, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Gαo2 did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
claims.source: Equally to the Gαi subunits, overexpression of Gαo1 (Figure 7c) or Gαo2 (Figure 7d) did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7d, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Gαq proteins did not reduce the TRPM3-evoked Ca2+ signals.
claims.source: Finally, also overexpression of Gαq proteins, which recently have been shown to influence TRPM8 channels (Zhang et al., 2012), did not reduce the TRPM3-evoked Ca2+ signals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: When Gβ1 and Gγ2 proteins were overexpressed together with TRPM3 channels, TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals were strongly reduced.
claims.source: However, when we overexpressed Gβ1 and Gγ2 proteins together with TRPM3 channels, TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals were strongly reduced (Figure 7e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7e, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The reduction of TRPM3 activity by Gβγ subunits was attenuated by the additional overexpression of (myristoylated) myr-βARKct, a Gβγ-binding peptide.
claims.source: Importantly, the reduction of TRPM3 activity by Gβγ subunits was attenuated by the additional overexpression of (myristoylated) myr-βARKct (Koch et al., 1994; Rishal et al., 2005), a Gβγ-binding peptide, indicating that the inhibition of TRPM3 channels was caused specifically by the overexpressed Gβγ subunits in an unbound state (Figure 7f,g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7f,g, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: A suppression of TRPM3 activity by overexpressed Gβγ subunits could also be demonstrated in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of transfected HEK cells.
claims.source: A suppression of TRPM3 activity by overexpressed Gβγ subunits could also be demonstrated in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of transfected HEK cells (Figure 7h,i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7h,i, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The peptide mSIRK caused a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons.
claims.source: Using this approach, we observed a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons as well as in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The peptide mSIRK caused a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells.
claims.source: Using this approach, we observed a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons as well as in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The inactive analog mSIRK-L9A did not cause a reduction in TRPM3 activity.
claims.source: The inactive analog mSIRK-L9A did not cause this effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: When Gβγ-binding peptides (myr-βARKct or myr-phosducin) were overexpressed, the inhibitory signaling from µORs to TRPM3 channels was severely reduced.
claims.source: When we tried to manipulate the concentration of free Gβγ subunits in the opposite direction by overexpression of Gβγ-binding peptides, myr-βARKct as before or myr-phosducin (Schulz, 2001; Rishal et al., 2005), we found that the inhibitory signaling from µORs to TRPM3 channels was severely reduced (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by free Gβγ dimers, but not by Gαi/o subunits.
claims.source: In aggregate, these data strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channels are inhibited by free Gβγ dimers, but not by Gαi/o subunits.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that overexpression of Gβγ inhibits TRPM3, while overexpression of Gα subunits does not, and that scavenging Gβγ reduces the inhibition.

claims.claim: Fused tags (YFP or myc) on TRPM3 proteins do not interfere with the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels, irrespective of their N- or C-terminal location.
claims.source: In control experiments, we determined that fused tags (YFP or myc) on TRPM3 proteins do not interfere with the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels, irrespective of their N- or C-terminal location (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, which shows experimental measurements.

claims.claim: The immunoprecipitation procedure precipitated full-length TRPM3 proteins.
claims.source: After separating the precipitated proteins, we observed a single band in western blots at the molecular weight expected for myc-TRPM3-YFP using antibodies against GFP, indicating that our procedure indeed precipitated full-length TRPM3 proteins (Figure 8a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8a, which shows a western blot.

claims.claim: Gβ co-precipitated with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells.
claims.source: When we probed blots with antibodies against Gβ subunits, we found evidence for Gβ co-precipitating with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8b,c, which shows western blots.

claims.claim: Using the same protocol on HEK cells without TRPM3 did not lead to precipitation of Gβ proteins.
claims.source: Using the same protocol on HEK cells without TRPM3 did not lead to precipitation of Gβ proteins (Figure 8b,c, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8b,c and Figure 8—figure supplement 2, which shows western blots.

claims.claim: In mass spectrometry experiments, peptide fragments belonging unequivocally to Gβ1 proteins were identified.
claims.source: Finally, in order to ascertain the identity of Gβ proteins interacting with TRPM3 without the potentially confounding issue of antibody specificity, we identified in mass spectrometry experiments peptide fragments belonging unequivocally to Gβ1 proteins. These peptides originated from trypsin-digested SDS gels containing proteins co-immunoprecipitating with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9, which shows mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: Gαi3 subunits were abundantly present in the cell lysates, but could not be detected on western blots of proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3.
claims.source: Although Gαi3 subunits were abundantly present in the cell lysates, we could not detect them on western blots of proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3 (Figure 8d; see also Figure 8—figure supplement 3a for tests of the antibodies against Gαi3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8d and Figure 8—figure supplement 3a, which shows western blots.

claims.claim: Gαq proteins were not detected co-precipitating with TRPM3.
claims.source: Because TRPM8 proteins have recently been shown to interact directly with Gαq proteins (Zhang et al., 2012), we also tested for, but failed to detect Gαq proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3 (Figure 8e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8e, which shows western blots.

claims.claim: TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are present in the same protein complexes.
claims.source: These data show that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are present in the same protein complexes.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data showing that Gβ proteins co-precipitate with TRPM3.

claims.claim: The presence of TRPM3 and Gβ proteins in the same protein complexes provides a mechanistic explanation for the inhibitory action of µORs exerted on TRPM3 channels.
claims.source: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the inhibitory action of µORs exerted on TRPM3 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data showing that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are in the same complex, combined with the functional data showing that Gβγ inhibits TRPM3.

claims.claim: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection.
claims.source: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs (Stein and Lang, 2009) strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection, but did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection (Figure 10a,b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10a, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claims.claim: Co-injection of DAMGO did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection.
claims.source: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs (Stein and Lang, 2009) strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection, but did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection (Figure 10a,b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10b, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claims.claim: Injecting higher concentrations of capsaicin into the hind paw produced considerably longer responses.
claims.source: Injecting higher concentrations of capsaicin into the hind paw produced considerably longer responses, showing that the lower capsaicin dose used in Figure 10b did not saturate the pain-evoked behavior under our conditions (Figure 10c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10c, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claims.claim: Co-injecting DAMGO was ineffective in reducing the duration of the capsaicin-induced nocifensive behavior at higher capsaicin doses.
claims.source: Again, co-injecting DAMGO was ineffective in reducing the duration of the capsaicin-induced nocifensive behavior at these higher capsaicin doses (Figure 10c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10c, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claims.claim: Locally, in the peripheral skin of living mice, TRPM3 channels, much more than TRPV1 channels, are under rapid inhibitory control of µORs.
claims.source: These data show that locally, in the peripheral skin of living mice, TRPM3 channels, much more than TRPV1 channels, are under rapid inhibitory control of µORs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that DAMGO reduces PS-induced pain but not capsaicin-induced pain.

claims.claim: TRPM3 channels are a major target of an intracellular signaling cascade initiated by activated µORs.
claims.source: We show here that TRPM3 channels, expressed in primary nociceptive neurons, are a major target of an intracellular signaling cascade initiated by activated µORs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that µOR activation strongly inhibits TRPM3 channels.

claims.claim: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by activated µORs strongly, rapidly and, reversibly.
claims.source: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by activated µORs strongly, rapidly and, reversibly (Figures 1 and 2a–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2a-c.

claims.claim: The combined data from pharmacological experiments, overexpression studies and biochemical interaction analyses strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channel complexes are inhibited by directly binding to Gβγ dimers, but not to Gα subunits.
claims.source: Mechanistically, the combined data from pharmacological experiments, overexpression studies and biochemical interaction analyses presented here strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channel complexes are inhibited by directly binding to Gβγ dimers, but not to Gα subunits.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that overexpression of Gβγ inhibits TRPM3, while overexpression of Gα subunits does not, and that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are in the same complex.

claims.claim: Binding to Gβγ is the mechanism with which µORs affect many other ion channels, like voltage-gated Ca2+ and GIRK channels.
claims.source: Binding to Gβγ is the mechanism with which µORs affect many other ion channels, like voltage-gated Ca2+ and GIRK channels (Bourinet et al., 1996; Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005; Heinke et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bourinet et al., 1996; Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005; and Heinke et al., 2011.

claims.claim: In the family of TRP ion channels, direct regulation by Gβγ appears not to be common.
claims.source: In the family of TRP ion channels, however, direct regulation by Gβγ appears not to be common.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only a few TRP channels have been reported to be regulated by Gβγ.

claims.claim: One report linked TRPA1 channel activation to Gβγ dimers liberated after activation of the GPCR MrgprA3.
claims.source: One report linked TRPA1 channel activation to Gβγ dimers liberated after activation of the GPCR MrgprA3 (Wilson et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2011.

claims.claim: µOR activation has neither an inhibition nor a pronounced activation effect on TRPA1 channels.
claims.source: We tested therefore, whether µOR activation has an effect on TRPA1 channels in DRG neurons, but observed neither an inhibition nor a pronounced activation of these channels.

results.result: μ-opioid receptor (μOR) agonists (morphine, DAMGO, herkinorin, loperamide) strongly and reversibly inhibit pregnenolone sulfate (PS)-induced Ca2+ signals in isolated mouse DRG neurons. This inhibition is rapid (1-2 min reversibility), blocked by the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone, and independent of the chemical nature of the μOR agonist.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 provide converging evidence from Ca2+ imaging experiments showing that multiple structurally distinct μOR agonists inhibit TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons. The data include appropriate controls (naloxone blockade, C28-C29) and demonstrate reversibility (C27), supporting the conclusion that μOR activation leads to TRPM3 inhibition.

results.result: In HEK cells overexpressing TRPM3 and μORs, morphine and DAMGO inhibit TRPM3 channels activated by PS, nifedipine, or heat. This inhibition requires μOR expression, as omitting μOR cDNA abolishes the effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 demonstrate successful reconstitution of the μOR-TRPM3 signaling pathway in a heterologous system. The inclusion of appropriate negative controls (cells expressing only TRPM3, C34) and testing multiple TRPM3 activation modes (chemical agonists and heat) strengthens the conclusion that μOR activation directly inhibits TRPM3.

results.result: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrate that μOR activation rapidly (<5 s) inhibits TRPM3 currents in both HEK cells and DRG neurons. The inhibition is voltage-independent (IC50 values at +80 mV and -80 mV do not differ) and at least partially reversible upon DAMGO washout.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 provide electrophysiological evidence confirming the Ca2+ imaging results. The rapid time course (<5 s), voltage independence (C38-C39), and reversibility (C41) are well-documented with appropriate controls. The dose-response analysis (C38) adds quantitative rigor.

results.result: Application of the μOR agonist DAMGO does not evoke outward currents in isolated DRG neurons, indicating that the reduction of PS-induced currents by μOR activation is not due to activation of K+ channels or K+ channel-dependent hyperpolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 address a potential confounding mechanism (K+ channel activation leading to hyperpolarization). The patch-clamp data (C42) directly test for outward currents and find none, supporting the inference that TRPM3 inhibition is not indirect via hyperpolarization (C43-C44).

results.result: 91.5% (562 of 614) of PS-sensitive DRG neurons are inhibited by DAMGO. Most DAMGO-sensitive neurons (83%, 465 of 562) also express functional TRPV1 channels (capsaicin-sensitive), suggesting that μOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition occurs predominantly in peptidergic nociceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 provide a comprehensive characterization of the DRG neuron populations responding to μOR activation. The large sample size (614 PS-sensitive neurons) and correlation with TRPV1 expression (C47-C48) support the conclusion about the neuronal subtype specificity. The size distribution analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) further validates the cell type identification.

results.result: TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons are inhibited by a variety of Gαi-coupled GPCRs (GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors, somatostatin receptors). The Gαq-coupled mGluR5 receptor produces only weak, non-recovering inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 demonstrate that TRPM3 inhibition is not specific to μORs but is a general property of Gαi-coupled GPCRs. The testing of multiple receptor types with appropriate agonists and the contrast with Gαq-coupled receptors (C56-C57) support the conclusion about the signaling pathway specificity.

results.result: μOR activation does not substantially inhibit TRPV1, TRPA1, or TRPM8 channels in the time frame investigated (2 min). Among TRP channels implicated in noxious thermoreception and inflammatory hyperalgesia, only TRPM3 displays substantial, rapid, and reversible inhibition during μOR activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 establish the specificity of μOR-mediated inhibition for TRPM3 among TRP channels. The testing in both native DRG neurons (C59-C61) and heterologous expression systems (C62-C64) with appropriate controls strengthens the conclusion. However, the 2-min time frame limitation should be noted, as longer-term effects (e.g., via cAMP/PKA) are not excluded.

results.result: Pertussis toxin (PTX) treatment, which disrupts Gi/o protein signaling, strongly reduces or almost completely abrogates the DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 channels in both DRG neurons and HEK cells overexpressing μORs and TRPM3. This implicates the classical Gαi/o signaling pathway in TRPM3 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 provide pharmacological evidence for Gi/o protein involvement using PTX, a well-established tool for disrupting Gi/o signaling. The consistent results in both native neurons and heterologous systems support the conclusion. However, PTX effects can be incomplete and may have off-target effects.

results.result: TRPM3 inhibition by μOR activation does not involve changes in cAMP concentration or downstream kinases. Manipulating cAMP levels (forskolin + IBMX) or blocking kinases (AMP-PNP, H89, KT5720, BIM) does not prevent μOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition. However, removing intracellular Mg2+ abolishes the inhibition, consistent with G-protein signaling (which requires Mg2+ for GTP binding).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 systematically rule out cAMP/PKA and other kinase pathways using multiple complementary approaches (pharmacological manipulation, kinase inhibitors, ATP analogs). The Mg2+ dependence (C72-C73) provides positive evidence for G-protein involvement. The convergence of multiple negative results (no effect of cAMP manipulation or kinase inhibitors) strengthens the conclusion, though some kinase inhibitors showed unexpected effects (noted in C75).

results.result: Overexpression of Gβγ subunits (Gβ1 and Gγ2), but not Gα subunits (Gαi1, Gαi2, Gαi3, Gαo1, Gαo2, Gαq), inhibits TRPM3 channels. The Gβγ-mediated inhibition is attenuated by Gβγ-binding peptides (myr-βARKct, myr-phosducin) and enhanced by the Gβγ-liberating peptide mSIRK. This suggests that TRPM3 channels are inhibited by free Gβγ dimers, not by Gα subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C89 provide strong evidence for Gβγ-mediated inhibition through overexpression studies, peptide scavenger experiments, and Gβγ-liberating peptides. The systematic testing of multiple Gα subunits (including constitutively active mutants) and the rescue experiments with Gβγ scavengers (C83, C88) support the conclusion. However, the mSIRK experiments (C85-C87) are complicated by increased baseline Ca2+ (noted in text), which may confound interpretation.

results.result: Co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry experiments demonstrate that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are present in the same protein complexes. Gβ1 peptides were identified by mass spectrometry in TRPM3 immunoprecipitates. Gα subunits (Gαi3, Gαq) were not detected in TRPM3 immunoprecipitates. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the inhibitory action of μORs on TRPM3 channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 provide biochemical evidence for TRPM3-Gβ interaction through co-immunoprecipitation (C92-C93) and mass spectrometry (C94). The negative results for Gα subunits (C95-C96) support the model of Gβγ-mediated inhibition. The use of appropriate controls (untransfected HEK cells) and multiple detection methods (Western blot, mass spectrometry) strengthen the conclusion. However, co-immunoprecipitation does not prove direct interaction and could reflect indirect association within a larger complex.

results.result: In vivo behavioral experiments show that co-injection of DAMGO with pregnenolone sulfate (PS) into mouse hind paws strongly reduces PS-evoked nocifensive behavior, but DAMGO does not significantly reduce capsaicin-evoked nocifensive behavior at any concentration tested. This demonstrates that TRPM3 channels, more than TRPV1 channels, are under rapid inhibitory control of peripheral μORs in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 provide crucial in vivo validation of the cellular findings. The selective inhibition of TRPM3-dependent (PS-evoked) but not TRPV1-dependent (capsaicin-evoked) pain supports the cellular data showing preferential TRPM3 inhibition. The dose-response control (C101-C102) demonstrates that the lack of capsaicin inhibition is not due to saturation. However, the sample sizes are relatively small (n=8-11 mice per condition), and only male mice were used.

results.result: TRPM3 channels in primary nociceptive neurons are a major target of μOR signaling. The inhibition is strong, rapid, and reversible, occurs via direct binding to Gβγ dimers, and is effective in peripheral nerve endings in vivo. This indicates that TRPM3 channels play an important role in the physiological control of nociceptor excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106, C127-C128 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing evidence from cellular, biochemical, and in vivo experiments. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (Ca2+ imaging, electrophysiology, biochemistry, behavior) strongly supports these conclusions. However, the claim that TRPM3 is a 'major' target is somewhat subjective and based on comparison with other TRP channels rather than a comprehensive assessment of all μOR targets.

results.result: The findings suggest that TRPM3 inhibition might be a viable strategy to combat pain, especially inflammatory hyperalgesia, and that pharmacologically inhibiting TRPM3 channels directly might be a feasible alternative to μOR agonists with potentially fewer adverse effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137 are largely speculative (C134, C136, C137 are explicitly marked as speculation). While the findings provide support for TRPM3 as a pain target, the claims about clinical viability and comparative safety are not directly tested in this study. The unremarkable phenotype of TRPM3-deficient mice (C137) provides some support, but clinical translation requires additional studies.

results.result: Background claims about μ-opioid receptors: μORs are widely expressed in the nociceptive system, their agonists are potent analgesics used for acute and chronic pain, but they cause significant adverse effects (addiction, tolerance, hyperalgesia, respiratory depression, fatal overdoses). μORs are located on peripheral nerve endings and can provide clinically meaningful analgesia when activated peripherally.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are background/context claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the rationale for studying peripheral μOR signaling and TRPM3 as a potential target.

results.result: Background claims about μOR signaling mechanisms: At central synapses, μOR activation inhibits L-type Ca2+ channels and activates K+ channels, and interacts with TRPV1 through diverse mechanisms. In peripheral nerves, μORs inhibit voltage-gated Na+ and HCN channels, activate K+ channels, and inhibit TRPV1 channels through various pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C18 are background claims supported by citations to published literature. These establish the known signaling mechanisms of μORs and provide context for the novel findings about TRPM3.

results.result: Background claims about TRPM3 channels: TRPM3 channels are expressed in primary nociceptive neurons, are divalent-permeable cation channels, play an important role in noxious heat sensation (being intrinsically thermosensitive), lead to CGRP release, and are implicated in inflammatory hyperalgesia. TRPM3 inhibitors exhibit anti-nociceptive properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are background claims supported by citations to published literature. These establish TRPM3 as a relevant pain target and provide rationale for investigating its regulation by μORs.

results.result: Discussion claims about Gβγ regulation of ion channels: Gβγ binding is the mechanism by which μORs affect many ion channels (voltage-gated Ca2+, GIRK channels), but direct regulation by Gβγ is not common in TRP channels. TRPA1 has been linked to Gβγ (though μOR activation does not affect TRPA1 in this study), and TRPM1 regulation by Gβγ has been reported but is controversial. TRPM8 is regulated by Gαq, not Gβγ.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C115 are discussion/context claims supported by citations to published literature and by the negative results for TRPA1 in this study (C110). These place the TRPM3 findings in the context of known ion channel regulation mechanisms.

results.result: TRPM3 does not bind to or is not regulated by Gα subunits, reinforcing the model that the main signaling pathway from μOR to TRPM3 channels is via Gβγ proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by the overexpression studies (Figures 7-8) showing no effect of Gα subunits and no co-immunoprecipitation of Gα with TRPM3. This reinforces the Gβγ-mediated mechanism.

results.result: Discussion claims about other peripheral μOR signaling pathways: Other pathways include PI3Kγ/NO for KATP channels, direct Gβγ activation of GIRK2 channels (absent in mouse but present in human DRG), and cAMP/PKA-mediated regulation of various channels including TRPV1. TRPM3 channels, in contrast to TRPV1, are largely unaffected by cAMP manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C124 are discussion claims supported by citations and by the experimental data in this study (C124, Figure 5e-h). These contextualize the TRPM3 findings relative to other known peripheral μOR signaling mechanisms.

results.result: Summary of in vivo findings: TRPM3-dependent pain (PS-evoked) was strongly suppressed by μOR agonists, while TRPV1-dependent pain (capsaicin-evoked) was not significantly attenuated at any concentration tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 summarize the behavioral data (Figure 10) and are directly supported by the experimental results. This is a restatement of the in vivo findings already evaluated above.

results.result: Discussion claims reiterating TRPM3 properties: TRPM3 channels are present in small-diameter nociceptor neurons and can release inflammatory mediators like CGRP.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are discussion claims supported by citations to published literature. These reiterate established TRPM3 properties in the context of discussing the implications of the findings.

results.result: Peripherally restricted μOR agonists can still exhibit pronounced adverse effects such as tolerance and constipation.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is a discussion claim supported by a citation (Stein, 2016). This provides context for why alternative approaches (e.g., TRPM3 inhibitors) might be valuable.
